<reason>Side A built a stronger consequentialist case, convincingly arguing that capping offsets would trigger "greenhushing"—firms abandoning net-zero pledges rather than facing impossible in-value-chain mandates—thereby eliminating billions in climate finance for verified external reductions. Side B effectively argued that "net-zero" should mean a trajectory of absolute reduction rather than an accounting equilibrium, but failed to rebut Side A's evidence that profit-driven firms would not fund external projects as uncredited philanthropy, leaving Side A's route to victory intact.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1-A4.6) exposed the central tension in Side B's case: the law regulates only a voluntary marketing label, not operations, meaning firms would exit the claim rather than transform. By contrasting Side B's celebrated "honest admission" with the resulting loss of all offset funding—while emissions continue—Side A demonstrated that the proposition sacrifices real atmospheric benefit for semantic purity.</best_rebuttal>
